claims.text: Introducing a gradient microstructure in a metal can enhance its strength.
Introducing a gradient microstructure can retain or improve a metal's ductility.
Gradient microstructures can overcome the strength-ductility trade-off associated with uniform microstructures.
A conventional coarse-grained alloy has limited strength-ductility performance under standard processing conditions.
Surface mechanical attrition treatment or shot peening can produce ultrafine grains near the surface while retaining coarser grains in the core.
Severe plastic deformation near the surface generates a grain-size gradient from the surface to the interior.
Grain refinement near the surface increases dislocation density.
The refined surface region strengthens the metal.
Coarser grains in the interior preserve ductility.
Combining a refined surface with a coarse-grained core produces a synergistic enhancement of strength and ductility.
Gradient-treated samples will have higher yield strength than untreated uniform samples in tensile testing.
Gradient-treated samples will have higher ultimate tensile strength than untreated uniform samples.
Gradient-treated samples will have comparable or greater elongation than untreated uniform samples.
Strengthening a conventional uniform coarse-grained alloy typically reduces its ductility.
The mechanical-property improvement depends on balancing surface refinement with core grain size.
An excessively large or excessively small deformation or gradient depth can diminish gains in strength or ductility.
Optimal strain rate, peening medium, and treatment time vary by alloy.
